title: Gandhi and King read him
hook: Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. both drew on this essay

segments.voice: Yesterday, civil disobedience, and your line: conscience first. Men first, subjects afterward. Where did you put conscience first? Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

Some sentences stay home. They're read once, in the town they were written in, and then they sleep on a shelf. Others get on ships. Thoreau's essay was written by a man who spent one night in a small-town jail and went berry picking the next morning. It's short. It's prickly. It argues with its own readers. And yet it turned up, years later, in the hands of a lawyer organizing Indians in South Africa, and later still, in the memory of a pastor in Montgomery, Alabama. Today, where the essay went, and what each reader did with it.
screen: `SOME SENTENCES STAY HOME.` → `THIS ONE GOT ON A SHIP.` → `SOUTH AFRICA. MONTGOMERY.`

segments.voice: First, Gandhi. In South Africa, Gandhi was leading Indians in refusing unjust laws, and he came across Thoreau's essay. He later wrote that the resistance there was already well under way before he read it. But he borrowed Thoreau's phrase, civil disobedience, to explain the struggle to English readers. Then, he wrote, he found even that phrase didn't carry the whole meaning. Second, Gandhi's own word. In his account of those years he tells how the movement got its name: satyagraha, which he explained as holding firmly to truth, a force born of truth and love. So Thoreau's essay was a companion on that road, not its starting point. Third, King. Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that he first read the essay as a student and was fascinated by the idea of refusing to cooperate with an evil system. Later, as a pastor in Montgomery, during the bus boycott, he remembered it. He wrote that what the boycotters were saying came down to this: we can no longer lend our cooperation to an evil system. That's Thoreau's counter friction, carried onto a city bus. Fourth, each reader changed it. King wrote that the spirit of the movement came from Jesus's teaching of love, and its method from Gandhi. Gandhi grounded his in truth. Thoreau grounded his in conscience. Three people, three sources, one idea of open, peaceful refusal, passed from hand to hand. It traveled, and it didn't arrive unchanged.
screen: `GANDHI BORROWS THE PHRASE.` · `SATYAGRAHA: HOLDING TO TRUTH.` · `KING: NO COOPERATION WITH EVIL.` · then, large: `IT TRAVELED, AND CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line of it. Here is one, from the essay itself: let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine. Say it once, slowly, aloud or in your head. Settle and breathe. Then let it sit. Notice which word catches. Life. Friction. Machine. You don't have to agree with it. Just let it travel one more short distance, from the page into you, and see what it meets there. If it stirs a name, someone who once refused something for the right reason, hold them in mind too. The bell holds the time.
Gandhi and King read him. Thoreau's essay reached South Africa and Montgomery, and each reader made it their own. Today's word.
screen: `GANDHI AND KING READ HIM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it traveled. Today, pass one good sentence along to someone, a line you read, heard or were given, and let it go where it goes. Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Thoreau's essay is often read alongside Gandhi's and King's own writings, as one voice in a longer conversation about open, nonviolent refusal to cooperate with injustice.

fork.setup: you're Gandhi. you've borrowed Thoreau's phrase civil disobedience to explain your struggle, but it doesn't say everything. what do you do?
options: keep the phrase and stop explaining.
give the movement a name of its own: satyagraha.
fork.reveal: Gandhi explained satyagraha as holding firmly to truth, a force born of truth and love.

original.note: satyagraha, the name Gandhi gave his movement; he explained it as holding firmly to truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gandhi and King copied their ideas from Thoreau.
what it means: both read his essay and drew on it, each in his own way.
what a scholar hears: Gandhi wrote that his resistance predated his reading of Thoreau, and King credited Jesus for the movement's spirit and Gandhi for its method.

notes: All Gandhi and King material is paraphrased: their writings are not treated as public domain here. The practice line 'let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine' is Thoreau's, spoken without quotation marks; it was quoted and cited on day 1247.
